sentences.text: Campylognathoides, a rhamphorhynchoid pterosaur discovered in Lias deposits in Württemberg, derives its name from Greek words meaning "curved" and "jaw," referring to its curved lower jaw.
The snout ended in a slender point that curved slightly upward, while the skull was elongated with a lighter constitution compared to its contemporary Dorygnathus.
Its teeth were conical and recurved, featuring a broad base and a beveled inner point that formed a sharp cutting surface.
The largest specimen from Holzmaden, C. zitteli, possessed a wingspan of 1.75 meters.
In contrast, C. liasicus had a wingspan of three feet, making it significantly smaller than its contemporary C. zitteli.
The genus Campylognathoides was erected by Felix Plieninger based on better-preserved specimens found in the Holzmaden shale, with C. zitteli serving as the type species described in 1894.
Originally, the species P. liasicus was named by Friedrich August Quenstedt in 1858 based on wing fragments found near Metzingen.
A fossil collector later found a well-preserved pelvis in a slate quarry in Braunschweig, Germany, in 1986.

The upward-lateral position of the hip socket in the well-preserved pelvis found in a slate quarry in Braunschweig, Germany, in 1986, suggests the animal walked quadrupedally and could not stand erect on its hind legs.
A quadrupedal posture has been confirmed in other rhamphorhynchoid pterosaurs besides Campylognathoides.
Evidence from gut contents indicates that Campylognathoides ate the belemnoid cephalopod Clarkeiteuthis conocauda.
Researchers speculate that Campylognathoides had acute vision or a nocturnal lifestyle due to its large, low-placed eye sockets.

In 2003, David Unwin and Alexander Kellner established the clade Campylognathoididae, with Unwin placing it as the sister taxon to Breviquartossa within Lonchognatha, while Kellner placed it as the most basal branch within Novialoidea.
Although Kellner placed the clade as the most basal branch within Novialoidea, Unwin's placement as the sister taxon to Breviquartossa within Lonchognatha presents an alternative phylogenetic view.

Campylognathoides lived in Germany during the Early Jurassic, specifically the Early Toarcian age, in fossil sites located in the early Jurassic north of the Bohemian Massif island, situated in a shallow gulf of the Tethys Sea.
Campylognathoides lived during the Toarcian stage, between 184.2 and 182.9 million years ago.

In 2009, Padian argued that an erect posture was necessary for fast locomotion, creating a debate over whether the animal walked quadrupedally or bipedally, as he concluded that an upright posture was necessary for foot placement and that bipedal locomotion was a precondition for speed, despite the possibility of quadrupedalism.
In 2008, Padian noted that the difference in wing length between species might result from ontogenetic development, as larger individuals would need larger wings to limit wing loading.
Kevin Padian considers C. indicus a nomen dubium, suggesting it might be based on a fish fossil rather than a pterosaur.
The specialized fish-eating niche may have been filled by Dorygnathus, which is five times more common in these strata than Campylognathoides.
